sections.title: Headline
sections.content: A single paper on unifying partner and environment diversity for human-AI coordination is the only candidate with a verified or probable organization match in this daily window.

sections.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
sections.problem: Zero-shot coordination methods typically train agents to cooperate with diverse simulated partners in a fixed environment, leaving open whether jointly modeling partner and environment diversity improves coordination with novel partners in novel environments.
sections.method: The paper introduces Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across procedurally generated environments and then trains a cooperator policy against that partner population, adding a next-state prediction module to couple social and environmental reasoning.
sections.key_result: The authors report that CECP achieves the strongest performance among compared baselines and state-of-the-art results under their evaluation protocol on a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task and Overcooked under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions; they also report more interpretable latents, demonstrated by inference of partner skill levels.
sections.caveat: Results are as stated in the abstract under the authors' own evaluation protocol; no independent replication or external benchmark comparison is supplied. The Meta organization attribution is a probable author-line match, not a confirmed affiliation.
sections.why_it_matters: It targets the realistic setting where both the human partner and the environment are unseen, and links coordination performance to interpretable representations of partner behavior.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: The only paper meeting the organization-match bar is CECP, which jointly models partner and environment diversity for human-AI coordination. Its reported gains are under the authors' evaluation protocol, and the Meta affiliation is a probable author-line match rather than a confirmed one. No temporal comparison is supported by this single-day input.
